review:
Trash TV, developed by Lawrence Russell and published by Reverb Triple XP, is a curious and inventive indie platformer that takes a discarded relic of the past and breathes new life into it. The player assumes control of a sentient CRT television that awakens in a grim recycling plant, surrounded by heaps of broken electronics and industrial refuse. The TV’s singular goal is simple yet oddly endearing—to recover its lost remote control and restore itself to full functionality. From this modest premise, the game builds a darkly humorous journey through conveyor belts, compactors, and mechanical death traps, weaving platforming precision with puzzle-solving ingenuity. It is a story told almost entirely through atmosphere and environment, where the silence of the scrapyard says more than words could.

From the first moment, Trash TV establishes a distinctive identity with its visual and thematic style. The environments are drenched in mechanical gloom, rendered with muted industrial tones punctuated by glowing screens and flickering lights. The game’s protagonist—an old, boxy TV set—feels both nostalgic and melancholic, a relic of the past now fighting to survive in a world that has moved on. The grainy CRT distortion, static flickers, and occasional visual glitches are not just aesthetic choices; they form the essence of the experience, a constant reminder that you are literally playing as outdated technology. Combined with the moody ambient soundtrack and the quiet hum of machinery, the result is an atmosphere that feels both lonely and strangely alive, evoking the forgotten spirit of analog entertainment.

The gameplay fuses side-scrolling action with environmental puzzles, creating a rhythm that alternates between careful platforming and bursts of chaos. The controls are responsive and straightforward, giving the player the agility needed to navigate dangerous machinery and tight spaces. What sets Trash TV apart is its use of weaponry not merely for combat, but as an extension of puzzle mechanics. The TV can acquire a small arsenal—from pistols and Uzis to shotguns and even rocket launchers—and each weapon introduces a unique physical dynamic. For instance, firing certain weapons generates recoil that can be used to propel the TV upward or across gaps, transforming combat tools into creative mobility aids. This clever integration of physics into puzzle design provides a satisfying layer of discovery, ensuring that progression never becomes monotonous.

While the concept is solid, the structure of Trash TV is intentionally minimalistic. The game unfolds across a central hub leading to a handful of interconnected levels, each filled with traps, switches, and machinery puzzles that test your reflexes and timing. There is a clear sense of flow between levels, but the brevity of each section can catch players off guard. Many stages end abruptly, almost without fanfare, and the entire experience can be completed in under two hours. Yet that brevity works in its favor—it never overstays its welcome or falls into repetition. Each level introduces a new mechanic or twist, maintaining a sense of momentum that keeps players curious about what lies ahead. This is not a game designed for lengthy marathons but rather for a single, concentrated playthrough that delivers satisfaction in short bursts.

That said, the limited scope does expose the game’s rough edges. The puzzles, while well-designed, rarely reach the level of challenge seen in genre heavyweights like Super Meat Boy or Celeste. Some players may find the solutions too straightforward or the obstacles too forgiving, while others might appreciate the relaxed pacing and accessible difficulty. There are occasional quirks in pacing and design, such as checkpoints that reset progress unexpectedly or areas that end without clear resolution. Yet even in its imperfections, the game retains charm through its personality and inventiveness. It feels like the work of a developer deeply passionate about giving a discarded object a new voice, and that sincerity radiates through every level.

Trash TV’s greatest strength lies in how it conveys emotion without dialogue. The protagonist, a mute television set, somehow evokes empathy through its plight, its flickering screen almost expressive in its silence. The surrounding world—a desolate factory filled with the remnants of consumer electronics—becomes a metaphor for obsolescence and technological decay. There’s an understated melancholy beneath the surface humor, a quiet acknowledgment of how quickly innovation leaves old creations behind. Yet the TV’s determination to reclaim its identity transforms what could have been a grim tale into something subtly inspiring. It’s a reminder that even forgotten machines can have purpose and personality.

As an indie title, Trash TV does not attempt to compete with sprawling platformers or cinematic storytelling. Its ambition lies in mood, tone, and concept rather than length or complexity. For players who appreciate concise, creative experiences that experiment with familiar mechanics, it offers a compact but memorable journey. The fusion of retro aesthetics with modern design sensibilities gives it a timeless appeal, and its tight, polished controls ensure that every moment feels deliberate. It may not challenge the genre’s greats, but it doesn’t need to—it stands on its own as a quirky, atmospheric adventure that celebrates the spirit of indie creation. Trash TV may be short, but it leaves a lasting impression, transforming the life of an old television into a poetic reflection on obsolescence, persistence, and the strange beauty of forgotten technology.

Trash TV is a short snack-like experience. It has a good mixture of puzzles, platforming and combat which is contained in an charming visual style. It feels a bit like one of those games that came from nowhere and nobody played before it returned to nowhere, which is a shame because I'd say it's a good experience and somewhat graceful in it's simple gameyness. It's lacking in frills and pretensions and what you see what you get.

In some ways it is almost difficult to talk about because of how pared down the design is. Watching the trailer tells you everything about the game and while it's perhaps lacking in surprises it is a good example of a simple idea well executed.

It won't change your life, but most things don't and that doesn't make them any less worth enjoying. Just as how with food sometimes all we want is a PB&J at home - sometimes we want a simple game to kill a few hours. Trash TV delivers a solidly satisfying PB&J.

[b]Smash TV is a unique platformer-puzzler where the tools you use are guns. Had a lot of fun while playing it, but there are noticeable flaws and bug.[/b] 

For starters, [b]even with all your guns, combat is pointless.[/b] Enemies then to be either sponges or you get a ton of them thrown your way. Then [b]when you get hit, you loose control and start running left or right until you hit a wall, then you change directions. This last for around 5 seconds and the only thing you can do is jump.[/b] While this does work very well for a platformer, the combat is kinda dull, which is fine since its not the main point of the game.

Also the [b]losing control when you get hit could have been used in some really unique puzzles.[/b]

(For the guns keep in mind that combat is pointless, so only their functionality matters.)

[b]The games gives you 8 weapons: pistol, dual smg, shotgun, bolt gun, C4, archer's bow, machine gun, and tv remote.[/b] You start with the pistol, a simple pea shooter. The dual smgs are automatic weapons which you fire in both directions. This is literally used once and then its useless. The shotgun fires a spread of bullets and is 100% worthless. 

[b]The bolt gun can best be described as a sticky grenade launcher, and is also the most useful out of all the weapons. In this game you are imune to explosion damage but you still recieve the knockback. In the game, you use it for its aoe to destroy boxes and to jump over stuff with the aid of the knockback.[/b]

[b]The C4 is like the bolt gun but it drops C4 on the ground which you can explode by holding down the fire button (which was not well explained). It allows the same freedom of movement like the bolt gun except you no longer need a wall.[/b] It can also obviously be detonated remotely, which is used in some puzzles.

The archer's bow and the machine gun both seem to be optional. The archer's bow fires in an arc, powering up the longer you charge it, and eventually gains the ability to pierce. A feature that is only needed once in its area. The bow is also useless. The machine seems to be locked behind a puzzle that requires the archers bow, but it can be aquired with the bolt gun because of an obvious bug. The machine gun is an automatic gun that fires in one direction and constantly applies knockback when you fire. The knockback would be useful in a few areas to gain speed but the explosive weapons are much more useful.

The tv remote is a weapon that lets you switch between two versions of the room. It is the last one you get and is only used in 2 sections. It's potential is kinda wasted since its is only really used to switch around the platforms in the room.

[b]So, out of all 8 guns only the pistol, bolt gun, the c4, and the tv remote is ever used. The game would have been a lot better if it focused on weapons that expand your movement options instead of useless guns that are used for one puzzle.[/b]

[b]There are also noticable bugs in the end portion of the game.[/b] Examples include: tv remote not correctly switching platforms is some areas off the beaten path; game literally crashing if you use the remote in what I think is a secret area; a in game QR code does not work, either becasue of poor contrast or some other reason; mechanical noise not cutting out during the ending. [b]Most of these are excusable since they easily avoided.

Also the game ends abruptly.

Overall, it was a very good puzzle-platformer and I wish there was more.[/b]

You're a damaged TV, miraculously revived, trying to escape a rubbish processing facility. This is largely done by puzzling your way though rooms, frequently by triggering switches to (de)activate lasers, moving platforms, barriers, etc. And careful jumping.

Amass an arsenal of conventional weapons and heavy munitions! Soon realise you won't get to use them in a proper fight against enemies. I think this is meant to be ironic. They're mainly tools for solving puzzles. Like, by spraying bullets for clearing away trash, or exploding to let you jump further.

The dumb automaton enemies aren't proper opponents. Because they don't seem to actually, y'know, oppose you. They're fine for what they are, placed as obstacles, as elements in the puzzles. Their contact with you has an interesting effect which was a cool touch: you temporarily lose control and behave like a walking drone, like them. Plus analogue TV-style visual distortions. Throughout the game, glitchy, static-like visual and sound effects abound.

The best parts are the time-limited action sequences, which can feel quite tense. It's a modern action game, so you've got instant restarts. You 'die' a lot. (Does that still trick gamers into thinking a game is hard?) This isn't a hard game, and rightly so. How much time do you want to spend in a dump? Fortunately it isn't like a huge sprawling castle, so it's not too long! It's about the right length, at under 2 hours.

一款看上去有点糟糕，实际上非常棒的平台小游戏。
玩家需要扮演一台废旧电视机，从垃圾处理厂中逃出去。游戏有一个类似十字路口的实验室，各个关卡在这个实验室的不同方位。每次通关完后就会重新回到实验室。
在游戏流程中玩家会收集到各种枪械装备，多数用于解谜而不是攻击敌人。事实上，《垃圾电视机》中的解谜要素要大于动作和射击要素。
如果用手柄的话，震动会非常带感。切换装备时可以用左摇杆迅速切到所需装备，这一点初上手时需要习惯。
获得装备后不会给予玩家如何使用的提示，但手感不错的玩家往往一秒就知道了使用的方法。这和本作中的谜题一样，看上去很难的样子，但不知为何解答的流程非常顺畅。
在各个小关通关后，按照作者的提示，应该还有一段隐藏的剧情。但我对这个剧情还有点疑问：
[spoiler] 我在地图左边进入隐藏关卡后，只看到平台高处有一个表明Exit的出口，但怎么到达一直没有头绪。另外还有一个标了？的木箱，也不知道怎么取得。只是在使用遥控器后游戏“崩溃”，我可以用手柄选择键“Exit”，不知道这是不是正式的结局。希望有真正打通关的玩家指正。	[/spoiler]
游戏的缺点是流程过短，许多非常棒的点子都没有展开，只能算是一个小品游戏。
总之，如果你是一个平台游戏爱好者，那么这款游戏在打折时不可不入。

How long are the levels? When can I finally reach a save checkpoint?

I was under the impression that this game would automatically save often, so I could play for a few minutes, then come back the next day and resume. NOPE! I still haven't hit the end of a level/checkpoint, which means I've had to replay the 30 min I played the day before, just to get back to where I thought I would have started. The "levels" seem unreasonably long, and don't give any suggestion as to how close you are to completing one. For this reason, I would not have recommended the game.

BUT, the game is really fun! The gameplay is super enjoyable, and each new room poses a new, unique puzzle. The game runs super smooth, and I overall just really enjoy playing the NEW puzzles. Replaying the levels (which for some reason was an implemented part of the game) is stupid and boring, though. 

Still recommend for the gameplay and creative puzzles. Just make sure you have an hour+ to play and hope you made it to a save checkpoint before closing the game.

[h1] Увлекательное путешествие престарелого телевизора[/h1]
  
Старый телик с кинескопом и электронно-лучевой трубкой попадает в центр утилизации. После приведения телевизора в чувство (весьма хитрым образом), на его экране загорается настроечная таблица и мы начинаем исследовать наше окружение и возможности нашего героя-телевизора. Сначала флешбеками нам показывают, что телевизору неплохо бы найти его пульт. Собственно в этом и состоит задача всей игры.
  
По ходу дела мы постепенно получаем оружие - пистолет, 2 узи, гранатомет и т.п. Игра представляет из себя платформер с головоломками, присутствуют враги (их мало и они не блещут разнообразием и интеллектом)). Саундтрек и эффекты заглючивания телевизора очень хороши. Геймплей интересен.

Игра разрабатывается еще с 2011г. И, судя по ранним роликам, планировалось сделать мультиплеер. К сожалению, мультиплеера нет, как и достижений и карточек стим. Потому моя оценка 8 из 10.
